input.question: How is it that an american agency (FCC) can give approval for Space-X's global internet with more than 4000 satellites in orbit around the globe. What gives this agency the authority to make this kinds of decisions?
input.ground_truth: There are no global space cops. That is, no global regulatory body for outer space activities. The Outer Space Treaty says "the activities of non-governmental entities in outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, shall require authorization and continuing supervision by the appropriate State Party to the Treaty" That means if you're an American company that wants to launch stuff, you have to get permission from the US government, if you're Chinese, from China, etc. Each nation is responsible for damage or harm caused by its citizens' stuff. In the US, that approval happens through the Federal Aviation Administration, which regulates the rocket launch, and the Federal Communications Commission, which regulates satellite radio communications, and orbits to the extent that they affect communications. To my knowledge, nobody regulates the actual "being in space" part of it.

The FCC’s job is to make sure everyone plays fair and doesn’t bump into each other or break the rules. So, when Space-X wants to put lots and lots of satellites (like toys) in the sky to give internet to everyone, the FCC checks and says, “Yes, you can do that, but you have to follow these rules so nobody gets hurt or confused.”

The FCC can do this because the law says it’s their job to watch over things that happen in the sky above the United States, and also things that affect people in the United States, even if the satellites are far away. So, they decide if Space-X can put their satellites up there and how they should play nicely with everyone else.

In short: The FCC is like a playground monitor who makes sure everyone follows the rules when playing in the sky. That’s why they can say yes or no to Space-X putting up their satellites.
